text: You have a cleaned dataset, tested code, two answered questions, and a chart. But an analysis nobody understands changes nothing, and a project nobody can find doesn't help your career. This final lesson turns your work into a story a busy stakeholder will act on, and a portfolio piece a hiring manager can evaluate in five minutes.

Stakeholders don't want your process, they want your conclusion, then the evidence. A useful structure: headline — one sentence that answers the question; evidence — two or three numbers or one chart; so what — the action this suggests; caveats — what could make you wrong; and next steps — what you'd do with more time or data.

Here's how our capstone reads. Headline: revenue is concentrated in the North region, in Electronics, and in Q4; discounts didn't increase items per order, and returns were higher on discounted orders. Evidence: about $184K from 1,267 completed orders, Q4 at 34.6% of revenue, average quantity flat around 3 in every band, return rates from 7.2% up to 12.6%.

So what: plan inventory and staffing ahead of Q4, and review whether deep discounts are worth their return cost. Caveats: the deepest discount band has only 103 orders, this is association, not proof of cause, and we dropped about 4% of deduplicated rows for invalid quantities. Next steps: test the discount effect with a proper experiment, and confirm the quantity rule with the shop. Notice that the caveats make the analysis more credible, not less.

Never retype numbers into a report by hand — compute them once, from the cleaned file. Building a summary dictionary straight from groupby calls prints orders: 1267, revenue: 183979, q4_share_pct: 34.6, top_region: North, top_category: Electronics. Because the raw data is seeded and the pipeline is code, rerunning it always reproduces these exact figures.

A README is the front door of your project — keep it short and scannable: the question, the data source, key findings up top, how to run it in four steps, and your assumptions and limits. Being honest that the data is illustrative is a strength — hiring managers value clear limits far more than inflated claims.

Before you publish, run through a checklist: a fresh clone plus the README steps reproduces your results; requirements.txt and seeds are in place; tests pass and cover your key cleaning functions; the notebook is clean and Restart & Run All succeeds; no secrets or private data anywhere in the repo; and the README leads with the answer and a chart.

Practice a five-minute walkthrough: the business question in 30 seconds, what was wrong with the data and how you handled it in a minute, the two findings with the chart in two minutes, caveats and next steps in a minute, then questions. In interviews, describe decisions rather than syntax — why you set a rule, how you tested it, what you'd check next. When you're ready, repeat the whole workflow on a real public dataset.

You started this course setting up Python, and you've finished with a tested, reproducible, end-to-end analysis. You can write Python for data work, use NumPy and pandas fluently, clean messy data, pull data from files, databases, and APIs, and structure your code so others can trust it. Next in the Data Scientist path: Statistics and Probability for Data Science — the reasoning behind how confident you can be in a difference like 7.2% versus 12.6%.
